title: Use makes perfect
paragraphs: It cannot be expected that argument and instruction, however willingly we surrender our belief to what we read, will carry us far enough to act on it, unless we also train and shape the soul by experience for the course we have designed it for. Otherwise, when the moment comes, it will find itself at a loss. That is why the philosophers most ambitious of excellence were not content to sit at home in retirement and ease, waiting for fortune to spring on them while they were raw and untried. They went out to meet her, deliberately throwing themselves into the proof of difficulties. Some gave up their wealth to practise a voluntary poverty; others sought out labour and a harsh way of life to harden themselves against hardship and inconvenience; others deprived themselves of their dearest organs, such as sight or the instruments of generation, lest a pleasure too sweet and too easy should soften and corrupt the steadiness of the soul.

But in dying, which is the greatest task we have to do, practice can give us no help at all. A man can fortify himself by habit against pain, shame, want, and other such accidents, but death is something we can only experiment with once, and we are all apprentices when we come to it. There have been men in antiquity who managed their time so well that they tried in death itself to taste and savour it, bending the full force of their minds to discover what this passage is; but none of them has come back to tell us the news:
"Nemo expergitus exstat, Frigida quem semel est vitai pausa sequuta."
["No one wakes again once the cold pause of life has overtaken him." — Lucretius, iii. 942]

Julius Canus, a noble Roman of rare constancy and virtue, had been condemned to death by that worthless creature Caligula. Among the many remarkable proofs he gave of his resolve, just as he was about to receive the executioner's stroke, a philosopher friend of his asked him: "Well, Canus, where is your soul now? What is she doing? What are you thinking of?" — "I was thinking," he answered, "of how to hold myself ready, with my faculties settled and fixed, to see whether in this short, quick instant of death I could catch the motion of the soul as she leaves the body, and whether she feels anything in the parting; so that, if I could, I might come back afterwards and report it to my friends." This man philosophises not just up to death but in death itself. What an extraordinary self-possession, what bravery of mind, to want his own death to be a lesson to him, and to have the leisure to think of other matters in such a moment:
"Jus hoc animi morientis habebat."
["He had this mighty power of mind even in dying." — Lucan, viii. 636.]

And yet I fancy there is a certain way of making death familiar to us, and of testing in some sort what it is. We can gain an experience of it which, if not complete and perfect, will at least not be useless, and may render us steadier and more assured. If we cannot overtake it, we may approach it and look at it; if we cannot reach the fort itself, we may at least scout the approaches. It is no accident that we are taught to consider sleep as a likeness of death. How easily do we pass from waking into sleep; with how little concern do we lose the knowledge of light and of ourselves. The capacity to sleep might seem useless and contrary to nature, since it strips us of all action and feeling — were it not that by sleep nature is teaching us that she has made us as much for dying as for living, and in the middle of life shows us the eternal state she has in store for us afterwards, to accustom us to it and take away our fear. But people who, by some violent accident, have fallen into a faint and lost all sense have, I think, come very near seeing the true and natural face of death. The moment of passage itself, in fact, is not to be feared for any pain or distress it brings, since feeling requires time, and the moment of death is so short and abrupt that it must be insensible. It is the approaches we have to fear, and those do fall within the range of experience.

Many things look larger in imagination than they turn out to be in fact. I have spent a good part of my life in perfect health — not just sound, but sprightly and full of vigour — and this state, so green and lively, made the idea of sickness terrifying to me; when I came actually to experience illness, I found the attacks faint and easy compared with what I had feared. I see it every day. If I am sheltered in a warm room on a stormy and tempestuous night, I wonder how anyone can live out of doors, and feel sorry for those caught in the fields; if I am out there myself, I have no wish to be anywhere else. Being shut up in a room I always imagined unbearable; but I was quickly inured to a week, then a month, of being so confined, in a weak, ailing, and dejected condition. And I have found that, in times of health, I felt much more pity for the sick than I now feel deserves to be felt for me when I am one. The force of imagination heightens nearly half the substance and reality of the thing. I hope that when I come to die I will find the same; that, when all is said, the trouble I take, the preparation and assistance I call in to face the blow, is more than the case warrants. Still, we cannot give ourselves too much advantage.

During the time of our third or second civil troubles (I do not quite remember which), I went out one day to take the air about a league from my house, which sits at the very centre of all the violence and mischief of the recent French civil wars. Thinking myself perfectly safe and so close to home that I had no need of better equipment, I had taken a horse with a comfortable pace but not much strength. On my way back, an occasion suddenly arose to use this horse for something he was not used to, and one of my retinue — a tall, hefty fellow on a strong German horse with a hard mouth, fresh and full of go — galloped up to play the brave and push ahead of the others, charging full speed in the very track I was on, crashing like a Colossus onto the small man and the small horse with such weight and momentum that he flipped us both over, heels in the air. The horse went down stunned by the fall; I lay stretched out ten or twelve paces beyond him, my face battered and broken, my sword (which had been in my hand) another ten paces further on, my belt smashed to pieces, with no more motion or sense than a log. That was the only swoon I have ever had in my life until that hour. Those with me, after trying every means they could to bring me round and concluding I was dead, picked me up in their arms and with great difficulty carried me home — about half a French league away. On the way, after I had been given up for dead for more than two hours, I began to stir and to draw breath. So much blood had pooled in my stomach that nature had to rouse her forces to discharge it. They set me on my feet, and I threw up a whole bucketful of clotted blood, as I did several more times along the road. This relieved me enough that I began to recover a little life, but so slowly and by such small steps that my first sensations were closer to the approaches of death than of life:
"Perche, dubbiosa ancor del suo ritorno, Non s'assicura attonita la mente."
["For the soul, still uncertain of its return, cannot in its stupor compose itself." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, xii. 74.]

The memory of this accident, which is firmly imprinted on my mind, presenting me so naturally with the image and idea of death, has in some way reconciled me to that grim adventure. When I first began to open my eyes, my sight was so confused, so weak, and so dim that I could distinguish nothing but the light:
"Come quel ch'or apre, or chiude Gli occhi, mezzo tra'l sonno e l'esser desto."
["Like a man who now opens, now closes his eyes, halfway between sleep and waking." — Tasso, Gerusalemme Liberata, viii. 26.]

As for the functions of the soul, they came back at the same pace and to the same degree as those of the body. I saw myself all bloody, my doublet stained from top to bottom with the blood I had vomited. The first thought that came into my head was that I had been shot through with a harquebuss, since a great many shots had been fired around us. It seemed to me that my life was just hanging on my lips, and I shut my eyes to help, as I thought, in pushing it out, taking pleasure in languishing and letting myself go. It was an impression that only skimmed the surface of my soul, as faint and weak as everything else, but really, far from being painful, it was mingled with the sweetness people feel when they slide into sleep.

I believe this is the very same state we see those people in who faint with weakness in the agony of death; we pity them without cause, supposing them tortured by sharp pains or that their souls are bearing painful thoughts. I have always held, against the common opinion and particularly against La Boétie, that those we see so subdued and stupefied at the approach of death, or overwhelmed by long illness, or felled by some sudden accident like a stroke or a fit of falling sickness,

"Vi morbi saepe coactus Ante oculos aliquis nostros, ut fulminis ictu, Concidit, et spumas agit; ingemit, et tremit artus; Desipit, extentat nervos, torquetur, anhelat, Inconstanter, et in jactando membra fatigat;"

["Often, struck down by the force of disease, someone falls before our eyes as if by a thunderbolt, foaming, groaning, his limbs trembling, his mind wandering, his sinews stretched, racked, gasping irregularly, wearing himself out in convulsions." — Lucretius, iii. 485.]

— or wounded in the head, whom we hear muttering and now and then groaning grievously — though we gather from these signs that they seem to retain some consciousness and that there are movements of the body — I have always believed, I say, that both body and soul are numbed and asleep,
"Vivit, et est vitae nescius ipse suae,"
["He lives, and does not know that he is alive." — Ovid, Tristia, i. 3, 12.]

and I could not believe that with so deep a stupefaction of the limbs and so great a failure of the senses, the soul could keep any power inwardly to take notice of herself; and therefore that they have no tormenting reflections to make them feel and consider the misery of their state, and consequently are not much to be pitied.

For my own part, I can imagine no state more unbearable and frightful than to have the soul lively and afflicted, with no way of expressing itself — like, say, men sent to execution with their tongues cut out first (except that, in this sort of dying, the most silent seems to me the most graceful, if accompanied by a grave and steady countenance); or like those wretched prisoners who fall into the hands of the brutal hangman-soldiers of our day, who torment them with every kind of inhuman treatment to force them to pay some impossible ransom, while keeping them, meanwhile, in a place and condition where they have no means of expressing or signalling their thoughts and misery. The poets imagined gods who favoured the deliverance of those undergoing a lingering death:
"Hunc ego Diti Sacrum jussa fero, teque isto corpore solvo."
["I, ordered to do it, bear this sacred thing as an offering to Pluto, and from that body release you." — Aeneid, iv. 782.]

Both the broken words and the short, irregular answers one sometimes gets out of such people by shouting and making a fuss around them, or the motions that seem to consent to what we want them to do, are no proof that they are alive in any full sense. The same thing happens to us, at the edge of sleep before it fully takes us, when we perceive as in a dream what is going on around us, and follow the last things being said with a confused and uncertain hearing that barely touches the borders of the soul, and we answer the last words spoken to us with replies that have more chance than sense in them.

Now, since I have actually tried it, I have no doubt that I have judged this rightly so far. For first of all, while I was in my swoon, I worked to rip open the buttons of my doublet with my nails — my sword was gone — and yet I felt nothing in my imagination that hurt me; for we have many movements in us that do not come from our direction:
"Semianimesque micant digiti, ferrumque retractant;"
["The half-dead fingers twitch, and grasp again at the sword." — Aeneid, x. 396.]
Likewise, people falling stretch out their arms before them by a natural impulse, which prompts our limbs to actions and motions without any orders from our reason.
"Falciferos memorant currus abscindere membra . . . Ut tremere in terra videatur ab artubus id quod Decidit abscissum; cum mens tamen atque hominis vis Mobilitate mali, non quit sentire dolorem."

["They tell of scythe-bearing chariots cutting off limbs, so that the severed limb is seen to quiver on the ground; and yet the mind of the man from whom it was cut, by the swiftness of the stroke, feels no pain." — Lucretius, iii. 642.]

My stomach was so loaded with the clotted blood that my hands moved to that part of their own accord, as they often do to a place that itches, without being directed by the will. There are several animals, and even human beings, in whom you can see the muscles twitch and quiver after they are dead. Everyone knows from experience that there are parts of us that stiffen or go limp without our permission. Now those passions which only touch the outer rind of us cannot really be called ours; for them to be ours, the whole man must take part, and the pains felt in the hand or the foot while we are asleep are none of ours.

As I drew near my house, where the news of my fall had already arrived ahead of me and my family had come out to meet me with the usual commotion, I not only made some short answer to their questions, but they tell me I was lucid enough to order them to bring a horse to my wife, whom I had seen on the road struggling and wearing herself out on the rough and hilly track. This would seem to come from a soul still doing its work, but it was nothing of the kind in me. I had no idea what I was saying or doing; these were idle clouds of thought stirred up by the sense-impressions of the eyes and ears, and they did not come from me. I did not know where I had come from or where I was going, nor was I able to weigh or take in what was said to me. They were only light effects produced by the senses out of habit; whatever the soul contributed was as in a dream, lightly grazed, licked, and dewed by the soft pressure of the senses. Even so, my condition was in truth very easy and quiet. I had no grief upon me, either for others or for myself; it was an extreme languor and weakness, without any kind of pain. I saw my own house but did not recognise it. When they had put me to bed I felt an indescribable sweetness in that rest; for I had been hauled and lugged about pitifully by those poor men, who had taken the trouble to carry me in their arms over a long and rough way and had several times worn themselves out in the process. They offered me various remedies, but I would take none, certain that I had been mortally wounded in the head. And in fact it would have been a very happy death: the weakness of my mind robbed me of the power of judging, and the weakness of my body of the power of feeling. I was letting myself slip away so sweetly, so gently, that I can hardly think of an action less troublesome than that was. But when I came back to myself and resumed my faculties:
"Ut tandem sensus convaluere mei,"
["When at last my lost senses recovered." — Ovid, Tristia, i. 3, 14.]

— which was two or three hours later — I suddenly felt myself in terrible pain, my limbs battered and bruised by the fall, and was so ill for two or three nights afterwards that I thought I was dying all over again, but a more painful death this time, having already taken myself for dead; and to this day I still feel the bruises of that terrible shock. I should not leave out that the last thing they could get into my head was the memory of the accident itself, and I had it told to me over and over — where I was going, where I had come from, what time of day the mishap had happened — before I could grasp it. As for the manner of my fall, that was hidden from me out of consideration for the man who had caused it, and other little stories were invented to cover it. But a long time afterwards, and the very next day on which my memory began to come back and to picture for me the state I was in at the instant I saw that horse driving full tilt at me (for I had glimpsed him at my heels and given myself up for gone, though the thought had been so sudden that fear had had no time to step in) — it seemed to me like a flash of lightning piercing my soul, and as if I had come back from the other world.

This long story about so slight an accident would seem pointless enough, were it not for what I have gained from it for my own use; for I really do find that to get acquainted with death there is no need to do more than approach it closely. Every man, as Pliny says, is a good teacher to himself, provided he is able to observe himself at close quarters. What I offer here is not a doctrine, it is my study; not someone else's lesson, but my own; and if I share it, that should not be taken badly, since what is useful to me may, perhaps, also be useful to another. As for the rest, I spoil nothing; I use nothing but my own. If I play the fool, it is at my own expense and nobody else's; it is a folly that will die with me, and that no one is going to inherit. We hear of only two or three of the ancients who walked this path, and even there I cannot say whether they did it in the same way, since I know nothing of them but their names. No one since has followed the track. It is a rough road, rougher than it looks, to follow a soul as wandering and uncertain as ours; to push into the dark depths of its tangled inner windings; to choose and seize so many small nimble motions. It is a new and unusual undertaking, and it draws us away from the common and most respected occupations of the world. For many years now my thoughts have had no other aim or focus than myself, and I have pried into and studied nothing but myself; or if I study anything else, it is to apply it to myself, or rather inside myself. And yet I do not think it a fault if, like other people who do the same with much less profitable subjects, I share what I have learned in this one, even though I am not very pleased with my own progress. There is no description so difficult, nor surely so useful, as that of oneself; and even there a man has to curl his hair and dress up to appear in public — and I am perpetually grooming myself, because I am eternally on my own description. Custom has made it improper to speak about oneself, and forbids it outright, out of hatred for the boasting that seems inseparable from any testimony men give about themselves:
"In vitium ducit culpae fuga."
["The avoidance of a mere fault often leads us into a greater one." Or: "The escape from a fault leads into a vice." — Horace, Ars Poetica, line 31.]

This is, instead of blowing the child's nose, cutting it off altogether. I think the cure is worse than the disease. But granting that it must be sheer presumption to entertain people with talk about oneself, still, pursuing my general design, I cannot refrain from an action that publishes this weakness of mine, nor conceal a fault which I not only practise but profess. To speak my mind freely, however, I think that the habit of condemning wine because some people get drunk on it is itself to be condemned; we can only abuse what is good in itself, and I believe that this rule only has the popular vice in view. These are bridles for calves, with which neither the saints — whom we hear speaking so freely about themselves — nor the philosophers, nor the theologians let themselves be curbed; and neither will I, who am as little of the one as the other. If they do not write of themselves expressly, at least when the occasion calls for it they do not hesitate to step out into the open. What does Socrates discourse on more than himself? To what does he more often direct and steer the conversation of his disciples, than to speak of themselves — not of the lesson in their book, but of the substance and motion of their souls? We confess ourselves religiously to God and our confessor; and to our neighbours, in front of everyone. But some will answer that there we say nothing but accusations against ourselves. Why then, we are saying everything; for our very virtue itself is faulty and porous. My trade and my art is to live; anyone who forbids me to speak according to my own sense, experience, and practice might as well order an architect to speak of building not from his own knowledge but from his neighbour's, by someone else's knowledge and not his own. If it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues, why does Cicero not prefer the eloquence of Hortensius, and Hortensius that of Cicero? Perhaps they mean that I should give testimony of myself by works and effects, not just by words. What I mostly paint is my thoughts, a subject without shape and incapable of producing visible results; it is all I can do to give it body in this airy form of the voice. The wisest and most devout men have lived in great care to avoid any showy effects. Effects would speak more of fortune than of me; they show their own face, not mine, and only uncertainly, by inference; they are samples of one particular virtue. I expose myself entire. It is a body in which, at a single view, the veins, muscles, and tendons all appear, each in its place — here the effects of a cold, there of a beating heart, very tentatively. I do not write my deeds; I write myself and my essence.

I think a man should be very careful how he rates himself, and equally conscientious in giving a true report — for better or worse — impartially. If I thought myself perfectly good and wise, I would shout it out for all to hear. To speak less of oneself than the truth warrants is folly, not modesty; to take a smaller coin than one's worth is, according to Aristotle, fainthearted and cowardly. No virtue helps itself out with falsehood; truth is never a matter for error. To say more about oneself than is really true is not always sheer presumption either; it is often, more than that, sheer folly: to be excessively pleased with what you are, and to fall into an indiscreet self-love, is in my opinion the heart of this vice. The most sovereign cure for it is to do the exact opposite of what those people recommend who, by forbidding men to speak of themselves, by the same act forbid them to think of themselves. Pride lives in the thought; the tongue can have only a very small part in it.

They imagine that to think of oneself is to be delighted with oneself, that to keep one's own company and converse with oneself is to indulge oneself too much; but this excess springs only in people who take a superficial view of themselves and devote their main attention to their affairs, who call it mere daydreaming and idleness to occupy oneself with oneself, and treat self-cultivation as a building of castles in the air, looking on themselves as on a third party, a stranger. If anyone is rapt by his own knowledge, looking only at those beneath him, let him just turn his eyes back to past ages, and his pride will be brought down when he finds so many thousand spirits there who trample him underfoot. If he is in flattering admiration of his personal valour, let him recall the lives of Scipio and Epaminondas — so many armies, so many nations that leave him far behind. No particular quality can rightly make a man proud, once he weighs in the same scale the many other weak and imperfect qualities he has, plus the nothingness of the human condition at large. Because Socrates alone had truly absorbed the precept of his god, "Know thyself," and by that study arrived at the perfection of taking himself for nothing, he alone was thought worthy of the title of sage. Whoever shall know himself in that way, let him say so boldly.
